svg.text: EXPLANATION · THE COACH IN PLAIN WORDS

text.tspan: Your hips moved toward the ball on the way down: 7% of your body height between address and
impact, where the rule starts at 4%. When the hips push forward, your body has to stand up to
make room, so the club arrives with less space to swing through. Contact often turns thin or
blocked. The likely cause is hip rotation: at impact your lead hip had turned 31°, where we
typically see about 45°. If the hips cannot turn, they slide toward the ball instead. It may feel
like you stay down, but at impact your hips have moved toward the ball. Next session: the wall
drill, slow, keeping your trail glute on the wall through impact. At home: the 90/90 hip
rotation, to give your hips room to turn.

svg.text: MOBILITY EXERCISE · FOR RESTRICTED HIP ROTATION

text.tspan: Set up with your backside touching a wall (or
golf bag). Make slow half swings, keeping
your trail glute on the wall through impact.
Sit with both knees bent to 90°, one leg in
front, one to the side. Keep your chest tall
and rotate slowly to switch sides.

NOTES · ASK THE COACH ABOUT THIS CARD
Answers are based only on this analysis.
Why does it feel like I’m staying down when I’m not?

text.tspan: Because your upper body barely changed: your posture angle moved only 6°, so it feels like you held your height. The change is lower
down. In the impact frame your hips are 7% of your body height closer to the ball than at address (confidence: high). Nothing touches you
when the hips slide, so you do not feel it. The wall drill gives you that feedback: if your trail glute leaves the wall before impact,
that is the same move.

svg.text: Should I change my grip too?
This analysis does not look at your grip, so I can’t tell you. That one is for a coach to check in person.
